core: Working definition of strategy: a plan of action a business uses to achieve its goals in the market — in plain terms, a plan for how the business will compete and succeed (attributed to CFI's business-strategy explainer).
Strategy versus tactics: the overall plan versus the specific actions that carry it out, with an original example (Harborline Bikes).
The three strategic levels — corporate, business, functional — each with one line (CFI corporate strategy and strategic planning).
The strategy process: assess, choose, execute, review — the general loop, each with one line (grounded in CFI's six-step strategic planning process).
The two strategic questions: where to compete and how to win (CFI portfolio 'where to play' + SBA market research and competitive analysis).
Mission (why the business exists / what it does) versus vision (where it wants to go), each named with one line (CFI mission and vision statements).
Honest framing: a strategy is a bet, not a guarantee (CFI: success today does not guarantee success tomorrow; Porter/HBR on the sustainability of advantage).
supporting: Strategy is not the same as operational effectiveness — doing the same activities better; Porter's classic HBR framing.
Strategic management runs formulation (assessment of resources, industry, internal operations) then implementation (deploying resources to meet objectives).
Strategic planning integrates departments (accounting and finance, marketing, human resources) to accomplish strategic goals — the functional level.
A business plan is the written roadmap for how to structure, run, and grow the business (SBA).
Market research finds customers and competitive analysis helps a business stand out; research reduces risk (SBA).

Portfolio theory and financial modeling — beyond this literacy lesson.

claims.claim: A business strategy is a complete plan of action a business uses to achieve its goals in the market; in plain terms, it is the plan for how a business will compete and succeed.
Strategy is not the same as operational effectiveness — being better at the same activities; strategy involves deliberate choices about how the business will compete.
A strategy is carried out through specific actions; the overall plan is the strategy, and the individual actions that put it into effect are the tactics.
Corporate strategy looks across all of a firm's businesses to decide where the firm will 'play' — which businesses to be in — while business strategy covers how an individual business competes.

Strategy is executed through the company's departments; strategic planning focuses on integrating departments such as accounting and finance, marketing, and human resources to accomplish the strategic goals.

Strategic management runs in two broad phases: formulation, which starts with assessing available resources, the competitive environment, and internal operations before a strategy is created, and implementation, which deploys resources and steers the company toward its objectives.

The strategy process is a loop: assess the situation, choose a direction, execute the plan, then evaluate the results and review and adjust the plan as conditions change; many companies review quarterly or annually.

The two core strategic questions are where to compete — which market and which customers — and how to win there; market research finds customers while competitive analysis helps a business stand out from rivals.

A mission statement defines what a company does and what purpose it serves — why the business exists; a vision statement describes what the company desires to achieve in the long run — where it wants to go.

A strategy is a bet, not a guarantee: it is built on the best available information about an uncertain future, and success today does not guarantee success tomorrow, which is why strategies are reviewed and adjusted.
A good business plan guides the owner through each stage of starting and managing the business and serves as a roadmap for how to structure, run, and grow it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is strategy mainly a planning routine (analysis and process) or fundamentally about making choices?
positions: CFI presents strategic planning as a systematic, step-by-step process whose benefits include better decisions even when a specific strategy fails (process view).
Porter (HBR, 1996) argues strategy is not operational effectiveness and involves deliberate choices about how to compete (choice view).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson merges the two: strategy is the set of deliberate choices (where to compete, how to win) made through a practical loop of assess, choose, execute, review. The process is the vehicle; the choices are the substance.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Mission and vision statements are sometimes used interchangeably in casual business writing.
positions: CFI's mission explainer: a mission statement defines what a company does and what purpose it serves.
CFI's vision explainer: a vision statement describes what the company desires to achieve in the long run.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the clean textbook split — mission is why the business exists today; vision is where it wants to go — and notes that in practice the two can blur.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's blanket framing that business strategy 'is a foundational concept in Introduction To Business' — generic boilerplate, not a sourced claim.
The draft's toolbox-drawer analogy ('Think of business strategy as a label on a toolbox drawer') — unsupported and generic; replaced with an original route-and-footsteps analogy.
The draft's claim that the lesson exists mainly so students can 'organize information' for later discussions — editorial boilerplate, not evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic machine draft with source-verified content: an attributed working definition of strategy, the strategy/tactics distinction, three strategic levels, the assess-choose-execute-review loop, the two strategic questions, mission vs vision, and the bet framing.
Removed the toolbox-drawer analogy and the 'label on a drawer' framing.
All examples are original (Harborline Bikes commuter-bike scenario) and none are copied from any source.
Sibling-owned depth (competitive advantage, business environment, entrepreneurship) is explicitly out of scope and referenced only as related topics.
